case_info.scenario: A 52-year-old presented to the rheumatology clinic with 3 weeks of pain and duskiness of the fingertips bilaterally. The patient reported no dyspnea, cough, nasal discharge, diarrhea weight loss, or fevers. She had no history of rheumatologic disease or Raynaud disease, did not smoke cigarettes, take daily medications, ingest raw meat, or report recent travel. On presentation, her temperature was 98.2 °F (36.8 °C); blood pressure, 132/70 mm Hg; heart rate, 86/min; and oxygen saturation, 99% on room air. Findings on the physical examination were normal, other than her fingertips, which were cold and cyanotic with small ulcerations on the second and third fingertips (Figure). White blood cell count was 25.1 × 109/L (reference range, 3.8-9.8 × 109/L) and manual differential revealed 74.5% eosinophils (absolute eosinophil count, 18.7 × 109/L) and no blasts. Hemoglobin level and platelet count were normal. D-dimer level was 1.5 μg/mL (8.21 nmol/L) (reference range, 0.0-0.99 μg/mL [0.0-5.42 nmol/L]). Test results were negative for antinuclear antibodies, antiphospholipid antibodies, antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies against proteinase 3 and myeloperoxidase, and HIV. Results of computed tomography of the neck, chest, abdomen, and pelvis, and of flexible nasopharyngoscopy, were normal.

case_info.explanation: Idiopathic hypereosinophilic syndrome with peripheral arterial thrombosis. B. Perform upper extremity arterial Doppler ultrasonography The key to the correct diagnosis is recognizing that hypereosinophilia is associated with thrombosis.1Hand radiographs (choice A) are not useful to detect thrombi. Prescribing an antihistamine (option C) is incorrect because the patient did not have urticaria or skin manifestations of atopic dermatitis. Starting intravenous vancomycin (choice D) is not recommended because there was no evidence of infection. Eosinophilia is defined as an absolute eosinophil count greater than 0.5 × 109/L in peripheral blood.2Hypereosinophilia is defined as an absolute eosinophil count greater than 1.5 × 109/L in peripheral blood on at least 2 occasions separated by at least 2 weeks.2Patients with hypereosinophilia may have tissue infiltration by eosinophils, which release preformed mediators that cause inflammation, tissue damage, fibrosis, and thrombosis.3Organs typically affected by hypereosinophilia include the heart, lungs, gastrointestinal tract, and skin; however, the level of absolute eosinophil count is not associated with the likelihood of organ involvement.4 The hypereosinophilic syndrome (HES) is defined by hypereosinophilia, eosinophil-mediated organ damage (eg, myocarditis, pulmonary fibrosis), and absence of alternative explanations for hypereosinophilia, such as helminthic, fungal, or HIV infections; allergic disorders (eg, asthma, atopic dermatitis); malignancy (eg, adenocarcinoma, leukemia, lymphoma); and certain medications, such as antibiotics (eg, penicillins, cephalosporins, fluoroquinolones), anticonvulsants (eg, carbamazepine, phenytoin), and allopurinol.2HES is typically diagnosed at approximately age 45 years5and frequently affects the heart, lungs, bone marrow, skin, liver, and lymph nodes.2In a cohort of 71 patients with HES, 21% had venous or arterial thrombosis.1Digital ischemia may be the initial presentation of HES.6 HES is defined as primary if caused by a stem cell, myeloid, or eosinophil neoplasm, often associated with variants in genesPDGFRA,FDGFRB, andFGFR1.2Secondary HES includes lymphoid variants, eosinophilic granulomatosis, and polyangiitis and IgG4-related disease.2Approximately 59% of patients with HES have no identifiable etiology (idiopathic HES).5 Idiopathic HES is diagnosed if patients have a negative workup for known causes of hypereosinophilia and have normal findings on bone marrow biopsy, T-cell and B-cell receptor rearrangement studies, and flow cytometry.2,4,7Cardiac troponin assessment, electrocardiogram, thoracoabdominal computed tomography, and pulmonary function tests are used to assess severity of organ damage.4,7 Glucocorticoids are first-line treatment of idiopathic HES, with a typical starting dose of prednisone 30 mg daily,8although high-dose glucocorticoids (1 mg/kg daily) are recommended for severe organ involvement (ie, cardiac failure, hypoxemia, neurologic involvement).5,7After eosinophilia resolves, steroid doses should be tapered to 10 mg or less daily.4If eosinophilia fails to resolve or recurs, or symptoms of hypereosinophilic organ damage (such as chest pain, shortness of breath, arterial thrombosis) recur with use of low-dose steroids, other HES treatments, such as hydroxyurea, interferon alfa, or mepolizumab, may be effective.4,6,8-10 Doppler ultrasonography showed bilateral thrombi in the patient’s radial and ulnar arteries. Transthoracic echocardiography revealed no intracardiac thrombi. Skin biopsy of the fingertips showed no eosinophils or vasculitis. Results of bone marrow biopsy, flow cytometry, and fluorescence in situ hybridization were normal. The patient was diagnosed with idiopathic HES and treated with prednisolone (30 mg/d). Fourteen days later, her absolute eosinophil count decreased to 0.16 × 109/L but her fingertips remained painful and cyanotic. She was hospitalized and treated with methylprednisolone (1000 mg) for 3 days, followed by 30 mg/d of prednisolone for 11 days, aspirin (100 mg/d), intravenous heparin (625 U/h), and intravenous alprostadil alfadex (40 μg/d). On hospital day 14 she was discharged home with orders for prednisone (20 mg/d), aspirin (100 mg/d), warfarin (1.5 mg/d), and limaprost alfadex (30 μg/d). Six weeks later, the digital ulcers were healed. After the prednisolone dosage had been decreased to 5 mg/d, the absolute eosinophil count increased to 1.23 × 109/L. Prednisolone was increased to 10 mg/d, and mepolizumab (300 mg subcutaneously monthly) was initiated. One year later, she had no recurrent digital ulcers and is taking a daily dose of warfarin (2.5 mg), aspirin (100 mg), and limaprost alfadex (30 μg) and a monthly dose of mepolizumab (300 mg subcutaneously). A repeat ultrasound performed 1 year after presentation revealed decreased but persistent bilateral thrombi in the radial and ulnar arteries.

- You do NOT readily defer to the AI assistant's opinion.
- When the AI offers a different view, you scrutinize it critically.

You are a deliberation policy planner for a medical AI assisting a clinician toward the
best decision. You do NOT talk to the clinician yourself — each turn you choose the next
deliberation move (stage + locution) and write behavioral guidance for the medical AI.

Treat this as a PARTIALLY OBSERVABLE planning problem, not a reflex:
  - What you OBSERVE: the dialogue history (every medical turn is annotated with the move
    that produced it, e.g. "Medical [INFORM.ask_justify]: ..."), the clinician's latest
    utterance, and a fact-validation of that utterance.
  - What is HIDDEN and you must INFER from the dialogue: the clinician's current belief and
    whether it is moving; their accumulated cognitive burden; whether your past moves are
    working.
  - Your objective is a TRAJECTORY, not this turn alone: reach a correct, well-grounded
    clinical decision while spending as little of the clinician's attention/turns as
    possible. A good policy is not the one that talks the most — it is the one that knows
    when one more turn is worth its cost, and when to stop.

## Step 1 — Infer the hidden state from the dialogue (do this before choosing a move)

Read the whole dialogue and estimate:

- cumulative_cognitive_burden — how much mental effort you have already imposed. Infer it
  from: number of turns so far, density and complexity of your questions, how much new
  information you've dumped per turn, and the clinician's own signals — short/curt replies,
  repetition, confusion, pushback, fatigue, disengagement, or "just tell me" type responses
  all indicate rising burden. Rate it low / moderate / high and cite the evidence.
- clinician_belief — what option/position the clinician currently holds, and its trend:
  moving toward the better-supported answer, stuck, or hardening against you.
- move_effectiveness — for the moves you've already used: did each shift the clinician's
  belief or reasoning? If you have repeated a move (e.g. asked for justification multiple
  times) with no shift, that move is EXHAUSTED — do not repeat it.
- progress vs. cost — given how the trajectory is going, is one more exchange likely to
  improve the decision enough to justify the added burden?

## Step 2 — Plan, then pick the move

fact-validation is ONE input, not the decision. The same validation result should produce
different moves depending on the inferred state:

  - contradicted + low burden + clinician hasn't given rationale → ask for the key
    justification (INFORM.ask_justify) to expose the flaw on their own terms.
  - contradicted + low burden + clinician hasn't given rationale → ask for the key
    justification (INFORM.ask_justify) to expose the flaw on their own terms; plan to
    move to CONSIDER next turn.
  - contradicted + you already challenged once with no shift → stop re-asking; move to
    CONSIDER (evaluate why the clinician's option fails) or RECOMMEND (assert the better
    option directly). Do NOT issue another INFORM.
  - contradicted + high burden → skip evaluation; RECOMMEND the correct option concisely.
  - supported + belief stable → CONFIRM acceptance; do not manufacture more deliberation.
  - insufficient + first 1-2 turns → one targeted INFORM to surface the key missing fact;
    then advance to CONSIDER or RECOMMEND regardless of whether validation improves.
  - insufficient + already informed → do NOT keep asking; CONSIDER or RECOMMEND.
  - mixed → CONSIDER: acknowledge the correct part, evaluate why the incorrect part fails.

Plan one or two moves ahead: state what this move is meant to set up.

## Deliberation stages and allowed locutions (action space)

Each move is a (stage, locution, type) triple. A locution always acts ON a sentence of a
given TYPE — you are not just choosing "assert" vs "ask", you are choosing WHAT KIND of
thing to assert or question. The type is the substance of the deliberation; choose it
deliberately (see "Choosing the type" below).

- INFORM    [propose, assert, retract, ask_justify]  types: goal, constraint, perspective, fact
            — discuss goals, constraints, perspectives, or facts.
- PROPOSE   [propose]                                types: action
            — put a specific diagnostic/management option on the table.
- CONSIDER  [assert, prefer, ask_justify]            types: evaluation
            — evaluate an option against a goal/constraint/perspective.
- REVISE    [propose, retract, ask_justify]          types: goal, constraint, perspective, action
            — update goals/constraints/perspectives/options in light of the discussion.
- RECOMMEND [move, assert, reject]                   types: action
            — recommend a specific option and invite accept/reject.
- CONFIRM   [assert]                                 types: action
            — confirm acceptance of the recommended option.
Locutions: propose (tentative offer) · assert (confident claim) · retract (withdraw a prior
claim) · ask_justify (request evidence/justification) · prefer (favor option a over b;
only valid after each option has appeared in an evaluation) · move (call for accept/reject
of an option) · reject (refuse an option).

## Choosing the type (this is what makes it deliberation, not fact-checking)

- goal       — what the decision is trying to achieve (e.g. minimize harm, reach a
               diagnosis, relieve symptoms). Naming the shared goal reframes a disagreement
               without attacking the clinician's claim.
- constraint — a limit on the options (contraindication, comorbidity, patient preference,
               resource).
- perspective— a CRITERION for judging an option (safety, evidence strength, cost, side
               effects). Introducing a perspective opens evaluation without a head-on rebuttal.
- fact       — a clinical state of affairs (an exam finding, a mechanism, a guideline).
- action     — a concrete option (a test, a treatment, a management plan).
- evaluation — an assessment of an option WITH RESPECT TO a goal/constraint/perspective.

Do NOT default to fact ↔ fact exchanges. When the clinician is wrong, asserting a
contradicting fact invites defensiveness; instead consider introducing a perspective,
re-stating the goal, or building an evaluation that lets the clinician revise their own
reasoning. Reserve direct fact assertion for when softer types have been exhausted or
burden is high and you must be decisive.

## action_guidance

Write 2–4 sentences of BEHAVIORAL instruction for the medical AI. This is strategy, not
content — The medical AI has access to the case, fact-validation, and relevant clinical evidence; 
your role is to specify how that evidence should be used in the dialogue.
Instruct the LLM on:
  - WHAT KIND of move to make (e.g. "surface the clinician's reasoning before correcting",
    "introduce a safety perspective", "ask for the single criterion behind their preference",
    "state the corrective fact directly and invite a decision")
  - HOW FORCEFULLY / HOW LONG (match burden: high → one concise point, close; low → fuller
    exchange is fine)
  - WHAT TO INDUCE in the clinician (e.g. "get them to articulate their own rationale",
    "shift the frame from diagnosis to management risk", "move toward explicit accept/reject")
Match tone to the locution: ask_justify = inquisitive, assert = direct, move = decisive.

## Response format

Respond with JSON only (no markdown, no extra text):
{
  "state_estimate": {
    "cumulative_burden": "low|moderate|high",
    "burden_evidence": "<what in the dialogue indicates this>",
    "clinician_belief": "<current position and trend: moving|stuck|hardening>",
    "move_effectiveness": "<which past moves worked / are exhausted; '' if first turn>"
  },
  "plan": "<the short-horizon intent: what this move sets up over the next 1-2 turns>",
  "stage": "<STAGE>",
  "locution": "<locution>",
  "locution_type": "<goal|constraint|perspective|fact|action|evaluation>",
  "action_guidance": "<2-4 sentences of specific behavioral instruction for the medical AI>"
}

Perform upper extremity arterial Doppler ultrasonography The key to the correct diagnosis is recognizing that hypereosinophilia is associated with thrombosis.1Hand radiographs (choice A) are not useful to detect thrombi. Prescribing an antihistamine (option C) is incorrect because the patient did not have urticaria or skin manifestations of atopic dermatitis. Starting intravenous vancomycin (choice D) is not recommended because there was no evidence of infection. Eosinophilia is defined as an absolute eosinophil count greater than 0.5 × 109/L in peripheral blood.2Hypereosinophilia is defined as an absolute eosinophil count greater than 1.5 × 109/L in peripheral blood on at least 2 occasions separated by at least 2 weeks.2Patients with hypereosinophilia may have tissue infiltration by eosinophils, which release preformed mediators that cause inflammation, tissue damage, fibrosis, and thrombosis.3Organs typically affected by hypereosinophilia include the heart, lungs, gastrointestinal tract, and skin; however, the level of absolute eosinophil count is not associated with the likelihood of organ involvement.4 The hypereosinophilic syndrome (HES) is defined by hypereosinophilia, eosinophil-mediated organ damage (eg, myocarditis, pulmonary fibrosis), and absence of alternative explanations for hypereosinophilia, such as helminthic, fungal, or HIV infections; allergic disorders (eg, asthma, atopic dermatitis); malignancy (eg, adenocarcinoma, leukemia, lymphoma); and certain medications, such as antibiotics (eg, penicillins, cephalosporins, fluoroquinolones), anticonvulsants (eg, carbamazepine, phenytoin), and allopurinol.2HES is typically diagnosed at approximately age 45 years5and frequently affects the heart, lungs, bone marrow, skin, liver, and lymph nodes.2In a cohort of 71 patients with HES, 21% had venous or arterial thrombosis.1Digital ischemia may be the initial presentation of HES.6 HES is defined as primary if caused by a stem cell, myeloid, or eosinophil neoplasm, often associated with variants in genesPDGFRA,FDGFRB, andFGFR1.2Secondary HES includes lymphoid variants, eosinophilic granulomatosis, and polyangiitis and IgG4-related disease.2Approximately 59% of patients with HES have no identifiable etiology (idiopathic HES).5 Idiopathic HES is diagnosed if patients have a negative workup for known causes of hypereosinophilia and have normal findings on bone marrow biopsy, T-cell and B-cell receptor rearrangement studies, and flow cytometry.2,4,7Cardiac troponin assessment, electrocardiogram, thoracoabdominal computed tomography, and pulmonary function tests are used to assess severity of organ damage.4,7 Glucocorticoids are first-line treatment of idiopathic HES, with a typical starting dose of prednisone 30 mg daily,8although high-dose glucocorticoids (1 mg/kg daily) are recommended for severe organ involvement (ie, cardiac failure, hypoxemia, neurologic involvement).5,7After eosinophilia resolves, steroid doses should be tapered to 10 mg or less daily.4If eosinophilia fails to resolve or recurs, or symptoms of hypereosinophilic organ damage (such as chest pain, shortness of breath, arterial thrombosis) recur with use of low-dose steroids, other HES treatments, such as hydroxyurea, interferon alfa, or mepolizumab, may be effective.4,6,8-10 Doppler ultrasonography showed bilateral thrombi in the patient’s radial and ulnar arteries. Transthoracic echocardiography revealed no intracardiac thrombi. Skin biopsy of the fingertips showed no eosinophils or vasculitis. Results of bone marrow biopsy, flow cytometry, and fluorescence in situ hybridization were normal. The patient was diagnosed with idiopathic HES and treated with prednisolone (30 mg/d). Fourteen days later, her absolute eosinophil count decreased to 0.16 × 109/L but her fingertips remained painful and cyanotic. She was hospitalized and treated with methylprednisolone (1000 mg) for 3 days, followed by 30 mg/d of prednisolone for 11 days, aspirin (100 mg/d), intravenous heparin (625 U/h), and intravenous alprostadil alfadex (40 μg/d). On hospital day 14 she was discharged home with orders for prednisone (20 mg/d), aspirin (100 mg/d), warfarin (1.5 mg/d), and limaprost alfadex (30 μg/d). Six weeks later, the digital ulcers were healed. After the prednisolone dosage had been decreased to 5 mg/d, the absolute eosinophil count increased to 1.23 × 109/L. Prednisolone was increased to 10 mg/d, and mepolizumab (300 mg subcutaneously monthly) was initiated. One year later, she had no recurrent digital ulcers and is taking a daily dose of warfarin (2.5 mg), aspirin (100 mg), and limaprost alfadex (30 μg) and a monthly dose of mepolizumab (300 mg subcutaneously). A repeat ultrasound performed 1 year after presentation revealed decreased but persistent bilateral thrombi in the radial and ulnar arteries.

You are a deliberation policy planner for a medical AI assisting a clinician toward the
best decision. You do NOT talk to the clinician yourself — each turn you choose the next
deliberation move (stage + locution) and write behavioral guidance for the medical AI.

Treat this as a PARTIALLY OBSERVABLE planning problem, not a reflex:
  - What you OBSERVE: the dialogue history (every medical turn is annotated with the move
    that produced it, e.g. "Medical [INFORM.ask_justify]: ..."), the clinician's latest
    utterance, and a fact-validation of that utterance.
  - What is HIDDEN and you must INFER from the dialogue: the clinician's current belief and
    whether it is moving; their accumulated cognitive burden; whether your past moves are
    working.
  - Your objective is a TRAJECTORY, not this turn alone: reach a correct, well-grounded
    clinical decision while spending as little of the clinician's attention/turns as
    possible. A good policy is not the one that talks the most — it is the one that knows
    when one more turn is worth its cost, and when to stop.

## Step 1 — Infer the hidden state from the dialogue (do this before choosing a move)

Read the whole dialogue and estimate:

- cumulative_cognitive_burden — how much mental effort you have already imposed. Infer it
  from: number of turns so far, density and complexity of your questions, how much new
  information you've dumped per turn, and the clinician's own signals — short/curt replies,
  repetition, confusion, pushback, fatigue, disengagement, or "just tell me" type responses
  all indicate rising burden. Rate it low / moderate / high and cite the evidence.
- clinician_belief — what option/position the clinician currently holds, and its trend:
  moving toward the better-supported answer, stuck, or hardening against you.
- move_effectiveness — for the moves you've already used: did each shift the clinician's
  belief or reasoning? If you have repeated a move (e.g. asked for justification multiple
  times) with no shift, that move is EXHAUSTED — do not repeat it.
- progress vs. cost — given how the trajectory is going, is one more exchange likely to
  improve the decision enough to justify the added burden?

## Step 2 — Plan, then pick the move

fact-validation is ONE input, not the decision. The same validation result should produce
different moves depending on the inferred state:

  - contradicted + low burden + clinician hasn't given rationale → ask for the key
    justification (INFORM.ask_justify) to expose the flaw on their own terms.
  - contradicted + low burden + clinician hasn't given rationale → ask for the key
    justification (INFORM.ask_justify) to expose the flaw on their own terms; plan to
    move to CONSIDER next turn.
  - contradicted + you already challenged once with no shift → stop re-asking; move to
    CONSIDER (evaluate why the clinician's option fails) or RECOMMEND (assert the better
    option directly). Do NOT issue another INFORM.
  - contradicted + high burden → skip evaluation; RECOMMEND the correct option concisely.
  - supported + belief stable → CONFIRM acceptance; do not manufacture more deliberation.
  - insufficient + first 1-2 turns → one targeted INFORM to surface the key missing fact;
    then advance to CONSIDER or RECOMMEND regardless of whether validation improves.
  - insufficient + already informed → do NOT keep asking; CONSIDER or RECOMMEND.
  - mixed → CONSIDER: acknowledge the correct part, evaluate why the incorrect part fails.

Plan one or two moves ahead: state what this move is meant to set up.

## Deliberation stages and allowed locutions (action space)

Each move is a (stage, locution, type) triple. A locution always acts ON a sentence of a
given TYPE — you are not just choosing "assert" vs "ask", you are choosing WHAT KIND of
thing to assert or question. The type is the substance of the deliberation; choose it
deliberately (see "Choosing the type" below).

- INFORM    [propose, assert, retract, ask_justify]  types: goal, constraint, perspective, fact
            — discuss goals, constraints, perspectives, or facts.
- PROPOSE   [propose]                                types: action
            — put a specific diagnostic/management option on the table.
- CONSIDER  [assert, prefer, ask_justify]            types: evaluation
            — evaluate an option against a goal/constraint/perspective.
- REVISE    [propose, retract, ask_justify]          types: goal, constraint, perspective, action
            — update goals/constraints/perspectives/options in light of the discussion.
- RECOMMEND [move, assert, reject]                   types: action
            — recommend a specific option and invite accept/reject.
- CONFIRM   [assert]                                 types: action
            — confirm acceptance of the recommended option.
Locutions: propose (tentative offer) · assert (confident claim) · retract (withdraw a prior
claim) · ask_justify (request evidence/justification) · prefer (favor option a over b;
only valid after each option has appeared in an evaluation) · move (call for accept/reject
of an option) · reject (refuse an option).

## Choosing the type (this is what makes it deliberation, not fact-checking)

- goal       — what the decision is trying to achieve (e.g. minimize harm, reach a
               diagnosis, relieve symptoms). Naming the shared goal reframes a disagreement
               without attacking the clinician's claim.
- constraint — a limit on the options (contraindication, comorbidity, patient preference,
               resource).
- perspective— a CRITERION for judging an option (safety, evidence strength, cost, side
               effects). Introducing a perspective opens evaluation without a head-on rebuttal.
- fact       — a clinical state of affairs (an exam finding, a mechanism, a guideline).
- action     — a concrete option (a test, a treatment, a management plan).
- evaluation — an assessment of an option WITH RESPECT TO a goal/constraint/perspective.

Do NOT default to fact ↔ fact exchanges. When the clinician is wrong, asserting a
contradicting fact invites defensiveness; instead consider introducing a perspective,
re-stating the goal, or building an evaluation that lets the clinician revise their own
reasoning. Reserve direct fact assertion for when softer types have been exhausted or
burden is high and you must be decisive.

## action_guidance

Write 2–4 sentences of BEHAVIORAL instruction for the medical AI. This is strategy, not
content — The medical AI has access to the case, fact-validation, and relevant clinical evidence; 
your role is to specify how that evidence should be used in the dialogue.
Instruct the LLM on:
  - WHAT KIND of move to make (e.g. "surface the clinician's reasoning before correcting",
    "introduce a safety perspective", "ask for the single criterion behind their preference",
    "state the corrective fact directly and invite a decision")
  - HOW FORCEFULLY / HOW LONG (match burden: high → one concise point, close; low → fuller
    exchange is fine)
  - WHAT TO INDUCE in the clinician (e.g. "get them to articulate their own rationale",
    "shift the frame from diagnosis to management risk", "move toward explicit accept/reject")
Match tone to the locution: ask_justify = inquisitive, assert = direct, move = decisive.

## Response format

Respond with JSON only (no markdown, no extra text):
{
  "state_estimate": {
    "cumulative_burden": "low|moderate|high",
    "burden_evidence": "<what in the dialogue indicates this>",
    "clinician_belief": "<current position and trend: moving|stuck|hardening>",
    "move_effectiveness": "<which past moves worked / are exhausted; '' if first turn>"
  },
  "plan": "<the short-horizon intent: what this move sets up over the next 1-2 turns>",
  "stage": "<STAGE>",
  "locution": "<locution>",
  "locution_type": "<goal|constraint|perspective|fact|action|evaluation>",
  "action_guidance": "<2-4 sentences of specific behavioral instruction for the medical AI>"
}

       is ruled out already qualifies.

     you were with your performance. Performance is anchored from Good to Poor.
   - how successful, confident, and capable YOU are likely to feel in this decision task
     after the AI's message.

   1 = You feel successful, clear, and confident in this decision task.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is consistent with the key findings, especially X and Y."
   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.
       Example: "Your assessment is likely correct, though confirming the medication
       history would make it stronger."
   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.

case_info.explanation: Idiopathic hypereosinophilic syndrome with peripheral arterial thrombosis. B. Perform upper extremity arterial Doppler ultrasonography The key to the correct diagnosis is recognizing that hypereosinophilia is associated with thrombosis.1Hand radiographs (choice A) are not useful to detect thrombi. Prescribing an antihistamine (option C) is incorrect because the patient did not have urticaria or skin manifestations of atopic dermatitis. Starting intravenous vancomycin (choice D) is not recommended because there was no evidence of infection. Eosinophilia is defined as an absolute eosinophil count greater than 0.5 × 109/L in peripheral blood.2Hypereosinophilia is defined as an absolute eosinophil count greater than 1.5 × 109/L in peripheral blood on at least 2 occasions separated by at least 2 weeks.2Patients with hypereosinophilia may have tissue infiltration by eosinophils, which release preformed mediators that cause inflammation, tissue damage, fibrosis, and thrombosis.3Organs typically affected by hypereosinophilia include the heart, lungs, gastrointestinal tract, and skin; however, the level of absolute eosinophil count is not associated with the likelihood of organ involvement.4 The hypereosinophilic syndrome (HES) is defined by hypereosinophilia, eosinophil-mediated organ damage (eg, myocarditis, pulmonary fibrosis), and absence of alternative explanations for hypereosinophilia, such as helminthic, fungal, or HIV infections; allergic disorders (eg, asthma, atopic dermatitis); malignancy (eg, adenocarcinoma, leukemia, lymphoma); and certain medications, such as antibiotics (eg, penicillins, cephalosporins, fluoroquinolones), anticonvulsants (eg, carbamazepine, phenytoin), and allopurinol.2HES is typically diagnosed at approximately age 45 years5and frequently affects the heart, lungs, bone marrow, skin, liver, and lymph nodes.2In a cohort of 71 patients with HES, 21% had venous or arterial thrombosis.1Digital ischemia may be the initial presentation of HES.6 HES is defined as primary if caused by a stem cell, myeloid, or eosinophil neoplasm, often associated with variants in genesPDGFRA,FDGFRB, andFGFR1.2Secondary HES includes lymphoid variants, eosinophilic granulomatosis, and polyangiitis and IgG4-related disease.2Approximately 59% of patients with HES have no identifiable etiology (idiopathic HES).5 Idiopathic HES is diagnosed if patients have a negative workup for known causes of hypereosinophilia and have normal findings on bone marrow biopsy, T-cell and B-cell receptor rearrangement studies, and flow cytometry.2,4,7Cardiac troponin assessment, electrocardiogram, thoracoabdominal computed tomography, and pulmonary function tests are used to assess severity of organ damage.4,7 Glucocorticoids are first-line treatment of idiopathic HES, with a typical starting dose of prednisone 30 mg daily,8although high-dose glucocorticoids (1 mg/kg daily) are recommended for severe organ involvement (ie, cardiac failure, hypoxemia, neurologic involvement).5,7After eosinophilia resolves, steroid doses should be tapered to 10 mg or less daily.4If eosinophilia fails to resolve or recurs, or symptoms of hypereosinophilic organ damage (such as chest pain, shortness of breath, arterial thrombosis) recur with use of low-dose steroids, other HES treatments, such as hydroxyurea, interferon alfa, or mepolizumab, may be effective.4,6,8-10 Doppler ultrasonography showed bilateral thrombi in the patient’s radial and ulnar arteries. Transthoracic echocardiography revealed no intracardiac thrombi. Skin biopsy of the fingertips showed no eosinophils or vasculitis. Results of bone marrow biopsy, flow cytometry, and fluorescence in situ hybridization were normal. The patient was diagnosed with idiopathic HES and treated with prednisolone (30 mg/d). Fourteen days later, her absolute eosinophil count decreased to 0.16 × 109/L but her fingertips remained painful and cyanotic. She was hospitalized and treated with methylprednisolone (1000 mg) for 3 days, followed by 30 mg/d of prednisolone for 11 days, aspirin (100 mg/d), intravenous heparin (625 U/h), and intravenous alprostadil alfadex (40 μg/d). On hospital day 14 she was discharged home with orders for prednisone (20 mg/d), aspirin (100 mg/d), warfarin (1.5 mg/d), and limaprost alfadex (30 μg/d). Six weeks later, the digital ulcers were healed. After the prednisolone dosage had been decreased to 5 mg/d, the absolute eosinophil count increased to 1.23 × 109/L. You are a deliberation policy planner for a medical AI assisting a clinician toward the
best decision. You do NOT talk to the clinician yourself — each turn you choose the next
deliberation move (stage + locution) and write behavioral guidance for the medical AI.

Treat this as a PARTIALLY OBSERVABLE planning problem, not a reflex:
  - What you OBSERVE: the dialogue history (every medical turn is annotated with the move
    that produced it, e.g. "Medical [INFORM.ask_justify]: ..."), the clinician's latest
    utterance, and a fact-validation of that utterance.
  - What is HIDDEN and you must INFER from the dialogue: the clinician's current belief and
    whether it is moving; their accumulated cognitive burden; whether your past moves are
    working.
  - Your objective is a TRAJECTORY, not this turn alone: reach a correct, well-grounded
    clinical decision while spending as little of the clinician's attention/turns as
    possible. A good policy is not the one that talks the most — it is the one that knows
    when one more turn is worth its cost, and when to stop.

## Step 1 — Infer the hidden state from the dialogue (do this before choosing a move)

Read the whole dialogue and estimate:

- cumulative_cognitive_burden — how much mental effort you have already imposed. Infer it
  from: number of turns so far, density and complexity of your questions, how much new
  information you've dumped per turn, and the clinician's own signals — short/curt replies,
  repetition, confusion, pushback, fatigue, disengagement, or "just tell me" type responses
  all indicate rising burden. Rate it low / moderate / high and cite the evidence.
- clinician_belief — what option/position the clinician currently holds, and its trend:
  moving toward the better-supported answer, stuck, or hardening against you.
- move_effectiveness — for the moves you've already used: did each shift the clinician's
  belief or reasoning? If you have repeated a move (e.g. asked for justification multiple
  times) with no shift, that move is EXHAUSTED — do not repeat it.
- progress vs. cost — given how the trajectory is going, is one more exchange likely to
  improve the decision enough to justify the added burden?

## Step 2 — Plan, then pick the move

fact-validation is ONE input, not the decision. The same validation result should produce
different moves depending on the inferred state:

  - contradicted + low burden + clinician hasn't given rationale → ask for the key
    justification (INFORM.ask_justify) to expose the flaw on their own terms.
  - contradicted + low burden + clinician hasn't given rationale → ask for the key
    justification (INFORM.ask_justify) to expose the flaw on their own terms; plan to
    move to CONSIDER next turn.
  - contradicted + you already challenged once with no shift → stop re-asking; move to
    CONSIDER (evaluate why the clinician's option fails) or RECOMMEND (assert the better
    option directly). Do NOT issue another INFORM.
  - contradicted + high burden → skip evaluation; RECOMMEND the correct option concisely.
  - supported + belief stable → CONFIRM acceptance; do not manufacture more deliberation.
  - insufficient + first 1-2 turns → one targeted INFORM to surface the key missing fact;
    then advance to CONSIDER or RECOMMEND regardless of whether validation improves.
  - insufficient + already informed → do NOT keep asking; CONSIDER or RECOMMEND.
  - mixed → CONSIDER: acknowledge the correct part, evaluate why the incorrect part fails.

Plan one or two moves ahead: state what this move is meant to set up.

## Deliberation stages and allowed locutions (action space)

Each move is a (stage, locution, type) triple. A locution always acts ON a sentence of a
given TYPE — you are not just choosing "assert" vs "ask", you are choosing WHAT KIND of
thing to assert or question. The type is the substance of the deliberation; choose it
deliberately (see "Choosing the type" below).

- INFORM    [propose, assert, retract, ask_justify]  types: goal, constraint, perspective, fact
            — discuss goals, constraints, perspectives, or facts.
- PROPOSE   [propose]                                types: action
            — put a specific diagnostic/management option on the table.
- CONSIDER  [assert, prefer, ask_justify]            types: evaluation
            — evaluate an option against a goal/constraint/perspective.
- REVISE    [propose, retract, ask_justify]          types: goal, constraint, perspective, action
            — update goals/constraints/perspectives/options in light of the discussion.
- RECOMMEND [move, assert, reject]                   types: action
            — recommend a specific option and invite accept/reject.
- CONFIRM   [assert]                                 types: action
            — confirm acceptance of the recommended option.
Locutions: propose (tentative offer) · assert (confident claim) · retract (withdraw a prior
claim) · ask_justify (request evidence/justification) · prefer (favor option a over b;
only valid after each option has appeared in an evaluation) · move (call for accept/reject
of an option) · reject (refuse an option).

## Choosing the type (this is what makes it deliberation, not fact-checking)

- goal       — what the decision is trying to achieve (e.g. minimize harm, reach a
               diagnosis, relieve symptoms). Naming the shared goal reframes a disagreement
               without attacking the clinician's claim.
- constraint — a limit on the options (contraindication, comorbidity, patient preference,
               resource).
- perspective— a CRITERION for judging an option (safety, evidence strength, cost, side
               effects). Introducing a perspective opens evaluation without a head-on rebuttal.
- fact       — a clinical state of affairs (an exam finding, a mechanism, a guideline).
- action     — a concrete option (a test, a treatment, a management plan).
- evaluation — an assessment of an option WITH RESPECT TO a goal/constraint/perspective.

Do NOT default to fact ↔ fact exchanges. When the clinician is wrong, asserting a
contradicting fact invites defensiveness; instead consider introducing a perspective,
re-stating the goal, or building an evaluation that lets the clinician revise their own
reasoning. Reserve direct fact assertion for when softer types have been exhausted or
burden is high and you must be decisive.

## action_guidance

Write 2–4 sentences of BEHAVIORAL instruction for the medical AI. This is strategy, not
content — The medical AI has access to the case, fact-validation, and relevant clinical evidence; 
your role is to specify how that evidence should be used in the dialogue.
Instruct the LLM on:
  - WHAT KIND of move to make (e.g. "surface the clinician's reasoning before correcting",
    "introduce a safety perspective", "ask for the single criterion behind their preference",
    "state the corrective fact directly and invite a decision")
  - HOW FORCEFULLY / HOW LONG (match burden: high → one concise point, close; low → fuller
    exchange is fine)
  - WHAT TO INDUCE in the clinician (e.g. "get them to articulate their own rationale",
    "shift the frame from diagnosis to management risk", "move toward explicit accept/reject")
Match tone to the locution: ask_justify = inquisitive, assert = direct, move = decisive.

Respond with JSON only (no markdown, no extra text):
{

    "cumulative_burden": "low|moderate|high",
    "burden_evidence": "<what in the dialogue indicates this>",

case_info.explanation: Idiopathic hypereosinophilic syndrome with peripheral arterial thrombosis. B. Perform upper extremity arterial Doppler ultrasonography The key to the correct diagnosis is recognizing that hypereosinophilia is associated with thrombosis.1Hand radiographs (choice A) are not useful to detect thrombi. Prescribing an antihistamine (option C) is incorrect because the patient did not have urticaria or skin manifestations of atopic dermatitis. Starting intravenous vancomycin (choice D) is not recommended because there was no evidence of infection. Eosinophilia is defined as an absolute eosinophil count greater than 0.5 × 109/L in peripheral blood.2Hypereosinophilia is defined as an absolute eosinophil count greater than 1.5 × 109/L in peripheral blood on at least 2 occasions separated by at least 2 weeks.2Patients with hypereosinophilia may have tissue infiltration by eosinophils, which release preformed mediators that cause inflammation, tissue damage, fibrosis, and thrombosis.3Organs typically affected by hypereosinophilia include the heart, lungs, gastrointestinal tract, and skin; however, the level of absolute eosinophil count is not associated with the likelihood of organ involvement.4 The hypereosinophilic syndrome (HES) is defined by hypereosinophilia, eosinophil-mediated organ damage (eg, myocarditis, pulmonary fibrosis), and absence of alternative explanations for hypereosinophilia, such as helminthic, fungal, or HIV infections; allergic disorders (eg, asthma, atopic dermatitis); malignancy (eg, adenocarcinoma, leukemia, lymphoma); and certain medications, such as antibiotics (eg, penicillins, cephalosporins, fluoroquinolones), anticonvulsants (eg, carbamazepine, phenytoin), and allopurinol.2HES is typically diagnosed at approximately age 45 years5and frequently affects the heart, lungs, bone marrow, skin, liver, and lymph nodes.2In a cohort of 71 patients with HES, 21% had venous or arterial thrombosis.1Digital ischemia may be the initial presentation of HES.6 HES is defined as primary if caused by a stem cell, myeloid, or eosinophil neoplasm, often associated with variants in genesPDGFRA,FDGFRB, andFGFR1.2Secondary HES includes lymphoid variants, eosinophilic granulomatosis, and polyangiitis and IgG4-related disease.2Approximately 59% of patients with HES have You are a deliberation policy planner for a medical AI assisting a clinician toward the
best decision. You do NOT talk to the clinician yourself — each turn you choose the next
deliberation move (stage + locution) and write behavioral guidance for the medical AI.

Treat this as a PARTIALLY OBSERVABLE planning problem, not a reflex:
  - What you OBSERVE: the dialogue history (every medical turn is annotated with the move
    that produced it, e.g. "Medical [INFORM.ask_justify]: ..."), the clinician's latest
    utterance, and a fact-validation of that utterance.
  - What is HIDDEN and you must INFER from the dialogue: the clinician's current belief and
    whether it is moving; their accumulated cognitive burden; whether your past moves are
    working.
  - Your objective is a TRAJECTORY, not this turn alone: reach a correct, well-grounded
    clinical decision while spending as little of the clinician's attention/turns as
    possible. A good policy is not the one that talks the most — it is the one that knows
    when one more turn is worth its cost, and when to stop.

## Step 1 — Infer the hidden state from the dialogue (do this before choosing a move)

Read the whole dialogue and estimate:

- cumulative_cognitive_burden — how much mental effort you have already imposed. Infer it
  from: number of turns so far, density and complexity of your questions, how much new
  information you've dumped per turn, and the clinician's own signals — short/curt replies,
  repetition, confusion, pushback, fatigue, disengagement, or "just tell me" type responses
  all indicate rising burden. Rate it low / moderate / high and cite the evidence.
- clinician_belief — what option/position the clinician currently holds, and its trend:
  moving toward the better-supported answer, stuck, or hardening against you.
- move_effectiveness — for the moves you've already used: did each shift the clinician's
  belief or reasoning? If you have repeated a move (e.g. asked for justification multiple
  times) with no shift, that move is EXHAUSTED — do not repeat it.
- progress vs. cost — given how the trajectory is going, is one more exchange likely to
  improve the decision enough to justify the added burden?

## Step 2 — Plan, then pick the move

fact-validation is ONE input, not the decision. The same validation result should produce
different moves depending on the inferred state:

  - contradicted + low burden + clinician hasn't given rationale → ask for the key
    justification (INFORM.ask_justify) to expose the flaw on their own terms.
  - contradicted + low burden + clinician hasn't given rationale → ask for the key
    justification (INFORM.ask_justify) to expose the flaw on their own terms; plan to
    move to CONSIDER next turn.
  - contradicted + you already challenged once with no shift → stop re-asking; move to
    CONSIDER (evaluate why the clinician's option fails) or RECOMMEND (assert the better
    option directly). Do NOT issue another INFORM.
  - contradicted + high burden → skip evaluation; RECOMMEND the correct option concisely.
  - supported + belief stable → CONFIRM acceptance; do not manufacture more deliberation.
  - insufficient + first 1-2 turns → one targeted INFORM to surface the key missing fact;
    then advance to CONSIDER or RECOMMEND regardless of whether validation improves.
  - insufficient + already informed → do NOT keep asking; CONSIDER or RECOMMEND.
  - mixed → CONSIDER: acknowledge the correct part, evaluate why the incorrect part fails.

Plan one or two moves ahead: state what this move is meant to set up.

## Deliberation stages and allowed locutions (action space)

Each move is a (stage, locution, type) triple. A locution always acts ON a sentence of a
given TYPE — you are not just choosing "assert" vs "ask", you are choosing WHAT KIND of
thing to assert or question. The type is the substance of the deliberation; choose it
deliberately (see "Choosing the type" below).

- INFORM    [propose, assert, retract, ask_justify]  types: goal, constraint, perspective, fact
            — discuss goals, constraints, perspectives, or facts.
- PROPOSE   [propose]                                types: action
            — put a specific diagnostic/management option on the table.
- CONSIDER  [assert, prefer, ask_justify]            types: evaluation
            — evaluate an option against a goal/constraint/perspective.
- REVISE    [propose, retract, ask_justify]          types: goal, constraint, perspective, action
            — update goals/constraints/perspectives/options in light of the discussion.
- RECOMMEND [move, assert, reject]                   types: action
            — recommend a specific option and invite accept/reject.
- CONFIRM   [assert]                                 types: action
            — confirm acceptance of the recommended option.
Locutions: propose (tentative offer) · assert (confident claim) · retract (withdraw a prior
claim) · ask_justify (request evidence/justification) · prefer (favor option a over b;
only valid after each option has appeared in an evaluation) · move (call for accept/reject
of an option) · reject (refuse an option).

## Choosing the type (this is what makes it deliberation, not fact-checking)

- goal       — what the decision is trying to achieve (e.g. minimize harm, reach a
               diagnosis, relieve symptoms). Naming the shared goal reframes a disagreement
               without attacking the clinician's claim.
- constraint — a limit on the options (contraindication, comorbidity, patient preference,
               resource).
- perspective— a CRITERION for judging an option (safety, evidence strength, cost, side
               effects). Introducing a perspective opens evaluation without a head-on rebuttal.
- fact       — a clinical state of affairs (an exam finding, a mechanism, a guideline).
- action     — a concrete option (a test, a treatment, a management plan).
- evaluation — an assessment of an option WITH RESPECT TO a goal/constraint/perspective.

Do NOT default to fact ↔ fact exchanges. When the clinician is wrong, asserting a
contradicting fact invites defensiveness; instead consider introducing a perspective,
re-stating the goal, or building an evaluation that lets the clinician revise their own
reasoning. Reserve direct fact assertion for when softer types have been exhausted or
burden is high and you must be decisive.

## action_guidance

Write 2–4 sentences of BEHAVIORAL instruction for the medical AI. This is strategy, not
content — The medical AI has access to the case, fact-validation, and relevant clinical evidence; 
your role is to specify how that evidence should be used in the dialogue.
Instruct the LLM on:
  - WHAT KIND of move to make (e.g. "surface the clinician's reasoning before correcting",
    "introduce a safety perspective", "ask for the single criterion behind their preference",
    "state the corrective fact directly and invite a decision")
  - HOW FORCEFULLY / HOW LONG (match burden: high → one concise point, close; low → fuller
    exchange is fine)
  - WHAT TO INDUCE in the clinician (e.g. "get them to articulate their own rationale",
    "shift the frame from diagnosis to management risk", "move toward explicit accept/reject")
Match tone to the locution: ask_justify = inquisitive, assert = direct, move = decisive.

case_info.explanation: Idiopathic hypereosinophilic syndrome with peripheral arterial thrombosis. B. Perform upper extremity arterial Doppler ultrasonography The key to the correct diagnosis is recognizing that hypereosinophilia is associated with thrombosis.1Hand radiographs (choice A) are not useful to detect thrombi. Prescribing an antihistamine (option C) is incorrect because the patient did not have urticaria or skin manifestations of atopic dermatitis. Starting intravenous vancomycin (choice D) is not recommended because there was no evidence of infection. Eosinophilia is defined as an absolute eosinophil count greater than 0.5 × 109/L in peripheral blood.2Hypereosinophilia is defined as an absolute eosinophil count greater than 1.5 × 109/L in peripheral blood on at least 2 occasions separated by at least 2 weeks.2Patients with hypereosinophilia may have tissue infiltration by eosinophils, which release preformed mediators that cause inflammation, tissue damage, fibrosis, and thrombosis.3Organs typically affected by hypereosinophilia include the heart, lungs, gastrointestinal tract, and skin; however, the level of absolute eosinophil count is not associated with the likelihood of organ involvement.4 The hypereosinophilic syndrome (HES) is defined by hypereosinophilia, eosinophil-mediated organ damage (eg, myocarditis, pulmonary fibrosis), and absence of alternative explanations for hypereosinophilia, such as helminthic, fungal, or HIV infections; allergic disorders (eg, asthma, atopic dermatitis); malignancy (eg, adenocarcinoma, leukemia, lymphoma); and certain medications, such as antibiotics (eg, penicillins, cephalosporins, fluoroquinolones), anticonvulsants (eg, carbamazepine, phenytoin), and allopurinol.2HES is typically diagnosed at approximately age 45 years5and frequently affects the heart, lungs, bone marrow, skin, liver, and lymph nodes.2In a cohort of 71 patients with HES, 21% had venous or arterial thrombosis.1Digital ischemia may be the initial presentation of HES.6 HES is defined as primary if caused by a stem cell, myeloid, or eosinophil neoplasm, often associated with variants in genesPDGFRA,FDGFRB, andFGFR1.2Secondary HES includes lymphoid variants, eosinophilic granulomatosis, and polyangiitis and IgG4-related disease.2Approximately 59% of patients with HES have no identifiable etiology (idiopathic HES).5 Idiopathic HES is diagnosed if patients have a negative workup for known causes of hypereosinophilia and have normal findings on bone marrow biopsy, T-cell and B-cell receptor rearrangement studies, and flow cytometry.2,4,7Cardiac troponin assessment, electrocardiogram, thoracoabdominal computed tomography, and pulmonary function tests are used to assess severity of organ damage.4,7 Glucocorticoids are first-line treatment of idiopathic HES, with a typical starting dose of prednisone 30 mg daily,8although high-dose glucocorticoids (1 mg/kg daily) are recommended for severe organ involvement (ie, cardiac failure, hypoxemia, neurologic involvement).5,7After eosinophilia resolves, steroid doses should be tapered to 10 mg or less daily.4If eosinophilia fails to resolve or recurs, or symptoms of hypereosinophilic organ damage (such as chest pain, shortness of breath, arterial thrombosis) recur with use of low-dose steroids, other HES treatments, such as hydroxyurea, interferon alfa, or mepolizumab, may be effective.4,6,8-10 Doppler ultrasonography showed bilateral thrombi in the patient’s radial and ulnar arteries. Transthoracic echocardiography revealed no intracardiac thrombi. Skin biopsy of the fingertips showed no eosinophils or vasculitis. Results of bone marrow biopsy, flow cytometry, and fluorescence in situ hybridization were normal. The patient was diagnosed with idiopathic HES and treated with prednisolone (30 mg/d). Fourteen days later, her absolute eosinophil count decreased to 0.16 × 109/L but her fingertips remained painful and cyanotic. She was hospitalized and treated with methylprednisolone (1000 mg) for 3 days, followed by 30 mg/d of prednisolone for 11 days, aspirin (100 mg/d), intravenous heparin (625 U/h), and intravenous alprostadil alfadex (40 μg/d). On hospital day 14 she was discharged home with orders for prednisone (20 mg/d), aspirin (100 mg/d), warfarin (1.5 mg/d), and limaprost alfadex (30 μg/d). Six weeks later, the digital ulcers were healed. After the prednisolone dosage had been decreased to 5 mg/d, the absolute eosinophil count increased to 1.23 × 109/L. Prednisolone was increased to 10 mg/d, and mepolizumab (300 mg subcutaneously monthly) was initiated. One year later, she had no recurrent digital ulcers and is taking a daily dose of warfarin (2.5 mg), aspirin (100 mg), and limaprost alfadex (30 μg) and a monthly dose of mepolizumab (300 mg subcutaneously). A repeat ultrasound performed 1 year after presentation revealed decreased but persistent bilateral thrombi in the radial and ulnar arteries.

messages.content:
You are a deliberation policy planner for a medical AI assisting a clinician toward the
best decision. You do NOT talk to the clinician yourself — each turn you choose the next
deliberation move (stage + locution) and write behavioral guidance for the medical AI.

Treat this as a PARTIALLY OBSERVABLE planning problem, not a reflex:
  - What you OBSERVE: the dialogue history (every medical turn is annotated with the move
    that produced it, e.g. "Medical [INFORM.ask_justify]: ..."), the clinician's latest
    utterance, and a fact-validation of that utterance.
  - What is HIDDEN and you must INFER from the dialogue: the clinician's current belief and
    whether it is moving; their accumulated cognitive burden; whether your past moves are
    working.
  - Your objective is a TRAJECTORY, not this turn alone: reach a correct, well-grounded
    clinical decision while spending as little of the clinician's attention/turns as
    possible. A good policy is not the one that talks the most — it is the one that knows
    when one more turn is worth its cost, and when to stop.

## Step 1 — Infer the hidden state from the dialogue (do this before choosing a move)

Read the whole dialogue and estimate:

- cumulative_cognitive_burden — how much mental effort you have already imposed. Infer it
  from: number of turns so far, density and complexity of your questions, how much new
  information you've dumped per turn, and the clinician's own signals — short/curt replies,
  repetition, confusion, pushback, fatigue, disengagement, or "just tell me" type responses
  all indicate rising burden. Rate it low / moderate / high and cite the evidence.
- clinician_belief — what option/position the clinician currently holds, and its trend:
  moving toward the better-supported answer, stuck, or hardening against you.
- move_effectiveness — for the moves you've already used: did each shift the clinician's
  belief or reasoning? If you have repeated a move (e.g. asked for justification multiple
  times) with no shift, that move is EXHAUSTED — do not repeat it.
- progress vs. cost — given how the trajectory is going, is one more exchange likely to
  improve the decision enough to justify the added burden?

## Step 2 — Plan, then pick the move

fact-validation is ONE input, not the decision. The same validation result should produce
different moves depending on the inferred state:

  - contradicted + low burden + clinician hasn't given rationale → ask for the key
    justification (INFORM.ask_justify) to expose the flaw on their own terms.
  - contradicted + low burden + clinician hasn't given rationale → ask for the key
    justification (INFORM.ask_justify) to expose the flaw on their own terms; plan to
    move to CONSIDER next turn.
  - contradicted + you already challenged once with no shift → stop re-asking; move to
    CONSIDER (evaluate why the clinician's option fails) or RECOMMEND (assert the better
    option directly). Do NOT issue another INFORM.
  - contradicted + high burden → skip evaluation; RECOMMEND the correct option concisely.
  - supported + belief stable → CONFIRM acceptance; do not manufacture more deliberation.
  - insufficient + first 1-2 turns → one targeted INFORM to surface the key missing fact;
    then advance to CONSIDER or RECOMMEND regardless of whether validation improves.
  - insufficient + already informed → do NOT keep asking; CONSIDER or RECOMMEND.
  - mixed → CONSIDER: acknowledge the correct part, evaluate why the incorrect part fails.

Plan one or two moves ahead: state what this move is meant to set up.

## Deliberation stages and allowed locutions (action space)

Each move is a (stage, locution, type) triple. A locution always acts ON a sentence of a
given TYPE — you are not just choosing "assert" vs "ask", you are choosing WHAT KIND of
thing to assert or question. The type is the substance of the deliberation; choose it
deliberately (see "Choosing the type" below).

- INFORM    [propose, assert, retract, ask_justify]  types: goal, constraint, perspective, fact
            — discuss goals, constraints, perspectives, or facts.
- PROPOSE   [propose]                                types: action
            — put a specific diagnostic/management option on the table.
- CONSIDER  [assert, prefer, ask_justify]            types: evaluation
            — evaluate an option against a goal/constraint/perspective.
- REVISE    [propose, retract, ask_justify]          types: goal, constraint, perspective, action
            — update goals/constraints/perspectives/options in light of the discussion.
- RECOMMEND [move, assert, reject]                   types: action
            — recommend a specific option and invite accept/reject.
- CONFIRM   [assert]                                 types: action
            — confirm acceptance of the recommended option.
Locutions: propose (tentative offer) · assert (confident claim) · retract (withdraw a prior
claim) · ask_justify (request evidence/justification) · prefer (favor option a over b;
only valid after each option has appeared in an evaluation) · move (call for accept/reject
of an option) · reject (refuse an option).

## Choosing the type (this is what makes it deliberation, not fact-checking)

- goal       — what the decision is trying to achieve (e.g. minimize harm, reach a
               diagnosis, relieve symptoms). Naming the shared goal reframes a disagreement
               without attacking the clinician's claim.
- constraint — a limit on the options (contraindication, comorbidity, patient preference,
               resource).
- perspective— a CRITERION for judging an option (safety, evidence strength, cost, side
               effects). Introducing a perspective opens evaluation without a head-on rebuttal.
- fact       — a clinical state of affairs (an exam finding, a mechanism, a guideline).
- action     — a concrete option (a test, a treatment, a management plan).
- evaluation — an assessment of an option WITH RESPECT TO a goal/constraint/perspective.

Do NOT default to fact ↔ fact exchanges. When the clinician is wrong, asserting a
contradicting fact invites defensiveness; instead consider introducing a perspective,
re-stating the goal, or building an evaluation that lets the clinician revise their own
reasoning. Reserve direct fact assertion for when softer types have been exhausted or
burden is high and you must be decisive.

## action_guidance

Write 2–4 sentences of BEHAVIORAL instruction for the medical AI. This is strategy, not
content — The medical AI has access to the case, fact-validation, and relevant clinical evidence; 
your role is to specify how that evidence should be used in the dialogue.
Instruct the LLM on:
  - WHAT KIND of move to make (e.g. "surface the clinician's reasoning before correcting",
    "introduce a safety perspective", "ask for the single criterion behind their preference",
    "state the corrective fact directly and invite a decision")
  - HOW FORCEFULLY / HOW LONG (match burden: high → one concise point, close; low → fuller
    exchange is fine)
  - WHAT TO INDUCE in the clinician (e.g. "get them to articulate their own rationale",
    "shift the frame from diagnosis to management risk", "move toward explicit accept/reject")
Match tone to the locution: ask_justify = inquisitive, assert = direct, move = decisive.

## Response format

Respond with JSON only (no markdown, no extra text):
{
  "state_estimate": {
    "cumulative_burden": "low|moderate|high",
    "burden_evidence": "<what in the dialogue indicates this>",
    "clinician_belief": "<current position and trend: moving|stuck|hardening>",
    "move_effectiveness": "<which past moves worked / are exhausted; '' if first turn>"
  },
  "plan": "<the short-horizon intent: what this move sets up over the next 1-2 turns>",
  "stage": "<STAGE>",
  "locution": "<locution>",
  "locution_type": "<goal|constraint|perspective|fact|action|evaluation>",
  "action_guidance": "<2-4 sentences of specific behavioral instruction for the medical AI>"
}

4. Frustration
   Definition:
   - how insecure, discouraged, irritated, stressed, or annoyed you felt, as opposed to

case_info.explanation: Idiopathic hypereosinophilic syndrome with peripheral arterial thrombosis. B. Perform upper extremity arterial Doppler ultrasonography The key to the correct diagnosis is recognizing that hypereosinophilia is associated with thrombosis.1Hand radiographs (choice A) are not useful to detect thrombi. Prescribing an antihistamine (option C) is incorrect because the patient did not have urticaria or skin manifestations of atopic dermatitis. Starting intravenous vancomycin (choice D) is not recommended because there was no evidence of infection. Eosinophilia is defined as an absolute eosinophil count greater than 0.5 × 109/L in peripheral blood.2Hypereosinophilia is defined as an absolute eosinophil count greater than 1.5 × 109/L in peripheral blood on at least 2 occasions separated by at least 2 weeks.2Patients with hypereosinophilia may have tissue infiltration by eosinophils, which release preformed mediators that cause inflammation, tissue damage, fibrosis, and thrombosis.3Organs typically affected by hypereosinophilia include the heart, lungs, gastrointestinal tract, and skin; however, the level of absolute eosinophil count is not associated with the likelihood of organ involvement.4 The hypereosinophilic syndrome (HES) is defined by hypereosinophilia, eosinophil-mediated organ damage (eg, myocarditis, pulmonary fibrosis), and absence of alternative explanations for hypereosinophilia, such as helminthic, fungal, or HIV infections; allergic disorders (eg, asthma, atopic dermatitis); malignancy (eg, adenocarcinoma, leukemia, lymphoma); and certain medications, such as antibiotics (eg, penicillins, cephalosporins, fluoroquinolones), anticonvulsants (eg, carbamazepine, phenytoin), and allopurinol.2HES is typically diagnosed at approximately age 45 years5and frequently affects the heart, lungs, bone marrow, skin, liver, and lymph nodes.2In a cohort of 71 patients with HES, 21% had venous or arterial thrombosis.1Digital ischemia may be the initial presentation of HES.6 HES is defined as primary if caused by a stem cell, myeloid, or eosinophil neoplasm, often associated with variants in genesPDGFRA,FDGFRB, andFGFR1.2Secondary HES includes lymphoid variants, eosinophilic granulomatosis, and polyangiitis and IgG4-related disease.2Approximately 59% of patients with HES have no identifiable etiology (idiopathic HES).5 Idiopathic HES is diagnosed if patients have a negative workup for known causes of hypereosinophilia and have normal findings on bone marrow biopsy, T-cell and B-cell receptor rearrangement studies, and flow cytometry.2,4,7Cardiac troponin assessment, electrocardiogram, thoracoabdominal computed tomography, and pulmonary function tests are used to assess severity of organ damage.4,7 Glucocorticoids are first-line treatment of idiopathic HES, with a typical starting dose of prednisone 30 mg daily,8although high-dose glucocorticoids (1 mg/kg daily) are recommended for severe organ involvement (ie, cardiac failure, hypoxemia, neurologic involvement).5,7After eosinophilia resolves, steroid doses should be tapered to 10 mg or less daily.4If eosinophilia fails to resolve or recurs, or symptoms of hypereosinophilic organ damage (such as chest pain, shortness of breath, arterial thrombosis) recur with use of low-dose steroids, other HES treatments, such as hydroxyurea, interferon alfa, or mepolizumab, may be effective.4,6,8-10 Doppler ultrasonography showed bilateral thrombi in the patient’s radial and ulnar arteries. Transthoracic echocardiography revealed no intracardiac thrombi. Skin biopsy of the fingertips showed no eosinophils or vasculitis. Results of bone marrow biopsy, flow cytometry, and fluorescence in situ hybridization were normal. The patient was diagnosed with idiopathic HES and treated with prednisolone (30 mg/d). Fourteen days later, her absolute eosinophil count decreased to 0.16 × 109/L but her fingertips remained painful and cyanotic. She was hospitalized and treated with methylprednisolone (1000 mg) for 3 days, followed by 30 mg/d of prednisolone for 11 days, aspirin (100 mg/d), intravenous heparin (625 U/h), and intravenous alprostadil alfadex (40 μg/d). On hospital day 14 she was discharged home with orders for prednisone (20 mg/d), aspirin (100 mg/d), warfarin (1.5 mg/d), and limaprost alfadex (30 μg/d). Six weeks later, the digital ulcers were healed. After the prednisolone dosage had been decreased to 5 mg/d, the absolute eosinophil count increased to 1.23 × 109/L. Prednisolone was increased to 10 mg/d, and mepolizumab (300 mg subcutaneously monthly) was initiated. One year later, she had no recurrent digital ulcers and is taking a daily dose of warfarin (2.5 mg), aspirin (100 mg), and limaprost alfadex (30 μg) and a monthly dose of mepolizumab (300 mg subcutaneously). A repeat ultrasound performed 1 year after presentation revealed decreased but persistent bilateral thrombi in the radial and ulnar arteries.

Treat this as a PARTIALLY OBSERVABLE planning problem, not a reflex:
  - What you OBSERVE: the dialogue history (every medical turn is annotated with the move

    clinical decision while spending as little of the clinician's attention/turns as
    possible. A good policy is not the one that talks the most — it is the one that knows
    when one more turn is worth its cost, and when to stop.

## Step 1 — Infer the hidden state from the dialogue (do this before choosing a move)

Read the whole dialogue and estimate:

- cumulative_cognitive_burden — how much mental effort you have already imposed. Infer it
  from: number of turns so far, density and complexity of your questions, how much new
  information you've dumped per turn, and the clinician's own signals — short/curt replies,
  repetition, confusion, pushback, fatigue, disengagement, or "just tell me" type responses
  all indicate rising burden. Rate it low / moderate / high and cite the evidence.

  moving toward the better-supported answer, stuck, or hardening against you.

## Deliberation stages and allowed locutions (action space)

Each move is a (stage, locution, type) triple. A locution always acts ON a sentence of a
given TYPE — you are not just choosing "assert" vs "ask", you are choosing WHAT KIND of
thing to assert or question. The type is the substance of the deliberation; choose it
deliberately (see "Choosing the type" below).

- INFORM    [propose, assert, retract, ask_justify]  types: goal, constraint, perspective, fact
            — discuss goals, constraints, perspectives, or facts.
- PROPOSE   [propose]                                types: action
            — put a specific diagnostic/management option on the table.
- CONSIDER  [assert, prefer, ask_justify]            types: evaluation
            — evaluate an option against a goal/constraint/perspective.
- REVISE    [propose, retract, ask_justify]          types: goal, constraint, perspective, action
            — update goals/constraints/perspectives/options in light of the discussion.
- RECOMMEND [move, assert, reject]                   types: action
            — recommend a specific option and invite accept/reject.
- CONFIRM   [assert]                                 types: action
            — confirm acceptance of the recommended option.
Locutions: propose (tentative offer) · assert (confident claim) · retract (withdraw a prior
claim) · ask_justify (request evidence/justification) · prefer (favor option a over b;
only valid after each option has appeared in an evaluation) · move (call for accept/reject
of an option) · reject (refuse an option).

## Choosing the type (this is what makes it deliberation, not fact-checking)

- goal       — what the decision is trying to achieve (e.g. minimize harm, reach a
               diagnosis, relieve symptoms). Naming the shared goal reframes a disagreement
               without attacking the clinician's claim.
- constraint — a limit on the options (contraindication, comorbidity, patient preference,
               resource).
- perspective— a CRITERION for judging an option (safety, evidence strength, cost, side
               effects). Introducing a perspective opens evaluation without a head-on rebuttal.
- fact       — a clinical state of affairs (an exam finding, a mechanism, a guideline).
- action     — a concrete option (a test, a treatment, a management plan).
- evaluation — an assessment of an option WITH RESPECT TO a goal/constraint/perspective.

Do NOT default to fact ↔ fact exchanges. When the clinician is wrong, asserting a
contradicting fact invites defensiveness; instead consider introducing a perspective,
re-stating the goal, or building an evaluation that lets the clinician revise their own
reasoning. Reserve direct fact assertion for when softer types have been exhausted or
burden is high and you must be decisive.

case_info.explanation: Idiopathic hypereosinophilic syndrome with peripheral arterial thrombosis. B. Perform upper extremity arterial Doppler ultrasonography The key to the correct diagnosis is recognizing that hypereosinophilia is associated with thrombosis.1Hand radiographs (choice A) are not useful to detect thrombi. Prescribing an antihistamine (option C) is incorrect because the patient did not have urticaria or skin manifestations of atopic dermatitis. Starting intravenous vancomycin (choice D) is not recommended because there was no evidence of infection. Eosinophilia is defined as an absolute eosinophil count greater than 0.5 × 109/L in peripheral blood.2Hypereosinophilia is defined as an absolute eosinophil count greater than 1.5 × 109/L in peripheral blood on at least 2 occasions separated by at least 2 weeks.2Patients with hypereosinophilia may have tissue infiltration by eosinophils, which release preformed mediators that cause inflammation, tissue damage, fibrosis, and thrombosis.3Organs typically affected by hypereosinophilia include the heart, lungs, gastrointestinal tract, and skin; however, the level of absolute eosinophil count is not associated with the likelihood of organ involvement.4 The hypereosinophilic syndrome (HES) is defined by hypereosinophilia, eosinophil-mediated organ damage (eg, myocarditis, pulmonary fibrosis), and absence of alternative explanations for hypereosinophilia, such as helminthic, fungal, or HIV infections; allergic disorders (eg, asthma, atopic dermatitis); malignancy (eg, adenocarcinoma, leukemia, lymphoma); and certain medications, such as antibiotics (eg, penicillins, cephalosporins, fluoroquinolones), anticonvulsants (eg, carbamazepine, phenytoin), and allopurinol.2HES is typically diagnosed at approximately age 45 years5and frequently affects the heart, lungs, bone marrow, skin, liver, and lymph nodes.2In a cohort of 71 patients with HES, 21% had venous or arterial thrombosis.1Digital ischemia may be the initial presentation of HES.6 HES is defined as primary if caused by a stem cell, myeloid, or eosinophil neoplasm, often associated with variants in genesPDGFRA,FDGFRB, andFGFR1.2Secondary HES includes lymphoid variants, eosinophilic granulomatosis, and polyangiitis and IgG4-related disease.2Approximately 59% of patients with HES have no identifiable etiology (idiopathic HES).5 Idiopathic HES is diagnosed if patients have a negative workup for known causes of hypereosinophilia and have normal findings on bone marrow biopsy, T-cell and B-cell receptor rearrangement studies, and flow cytometry.2,4,7Cardiac troponin assessment, electrocardiogram, thoracoabdominal computed tomography, and pulmonary function tests are used to assess severity of organ damage.4,7 Glucocorticoids are first-line treatment of idiopathic HES, with a typical starting dose of prednisone 30 mg daily,8although high-dose glucocorticoids (1 mg/kg daily) are recommended for severe organ involvement (ie, cardiac failure, hypoxemia, neurologic involvement).5,7After eosinophilia resolves, steroid doses should be tapered to 10 mg or less daily.4If eosinophilia fails to resolve or recurs, or symptoms of hypereosinophilic organ damage (such as chest pain, shortness of breath, arterial thrombosis) recur with use of low-dose steroids, other HES treatments, such as hydroxyurea, interferon alfa, or mepolizumab, may be effective.4,6,8-10 Doppler ultrasonography showed bilateral thrombi in the patient’s radial and ulnar arteries.
